title: Senior's toolkit: HTTP from the command line
summary: curl with the flags that find where time goes, test one backend behind a load balancer, and check headers and protocol versions.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: HTTP from the command line
steps.body: curl is the universal HTTP client: in every container, every CI runner and every incident channel. These are the flags that turn it from "fetch a page" into a debugger.

toolkit.what: Shows the whole exchange: DNS result, TCP connect, TLS handshake, request headers (`>`) and response headers (`<`).
flags: only add the response headers to the output

toolkit.what: Breaks one request into DNS, connect, TLS, time to first byte and total. Tells you whether a slow call is the network or the server.
flags: first byte back (server think time ends)
toolkit.example: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'dns %{time_namelookup} tcp %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total} code %{http_code}\n' https://api.example.com/orders

toolkit.what: Sends a request to one specific server while keeping the real name, so SNI, the certificate check and the Host header are all correct.
flags: pin the name to an address for this call
connect to another host name and port instead
only changes the header, not SNI: wrong for HTTPS
toolkit.when: one backend behind the load balancer misbehaves, or before a DNS cut-over

toolkit.what: The script and health-check form: fail on HTTP errors, stay quiet, never hang.
flags: exit 22 on 4xx/5xx (`--fail-with-body` also prints the body)
give up after 5 seconds in total

toolkit.what: A HEAD request: only headers. Quick check of `cache-control`, `content-type`, redirects and which server or CDN answered.
flags: HEAD instead of GET (some servers answer HEAD differently)
a real GET, print headers only

toolkit.what: Forces a protocol version and `%{http_version}` reports what was used. Checks that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are really on.
flags: HTTP/3 over QUIC, if your curl is built with it (`curl -V` lists `HTTP3`)

toolkit.what: Send a body from a file with the right content type. Reproduces a client's request exactly.
flags: body from a file (`--data-binary @file` keeps newlines)
curl 7.82+: sets the JSON content type and accept headers for you

steps.prompt: Match each `curl -w` variable to the moment it measures (seconds from the start).
pairs: first byte of the response arrived

steps.prompt: Users say the orders API is slow. `curl -w` prints `dns 0.004 tcp 0.015 tls 0.041 ttfb 2.870 total 2.912`. Where do you look next?
options: At the server: almost all the time is between TLS done and the first byte, so the app (or something it calls) is slow
At the network path, with mtr
steps.explain: DNS, TCP and TLS together took 41 ms. The 2.8 s gap before the first byte is the server working: look at its traces, database queries and downstream calls.

steps.prompt: One of four backends behind the load balancer returns 500s. They all serve `https://api.example.com`. How do you send a request to backend `10.0.4.23` only, with the certificate still checked?
steps.explain: `--resolve` keeps the URL's host name, so SNI and certificate checks match. `-k` turns checking off, and `-H Host` with an IP sends no SNI for the name, so TLS may fail or hit the wrong virtual host.

steps.prompt: A health check that fails on HTTP errors and never waits more than 5 seconds.
steps.explain: `-f` makes a 500 exit non-zero, so the check fails. `--max-time` caps the whole request. (`--connect-timeout` exists too, but only covers the connection.)

steps.prompt: Which flag do you reach for?
items: Find out whether DNS, TLS or the server is slow
Test the new server before switching DNS
See exactly which request headers curl sent
Hit one backend behind the load balancer
See why the TLS handshake fails
Graph time to first byte in a cron job

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Keep the `curl -w` timing line in your shell history or a `~/.curl-format` file and paste its output into every "it's slow" thread. Use `--resolve` to test a server before DNS points at it, and `-fsS --max-time` in every script and health check.
